title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Review: OLS Estimators
From last time, the OLS estimators are:
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\]
They are unbiased, linear, and the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (Gauss-Markov).
Today: What do the residuals tell us, and how do we estimate the unknown \(\sigma^2\)?

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of today you will be able to:

Define residuals and explain what they measure
State and prove the four properties of OLS residuals
Define RSS and explain its role in regression
Compute and interpret \(\widehat{\sigma}^2\) and \(\widehat{\sigma}\)

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text: Residuals

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
What are Residuals?
After fitting the model, the residual for observation \(i\) is:
\[e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i = y_i - \widehat{\beta}_0 - \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i\]
Residuals measure how far each observation falls from the fitted line:

\(e_i > 0\): observed value is above the fitted line
\(e_i < 0\): observed value is below the fitted line
\(e_i = 0\): observation falls exactly on the fitted line







Note


Residuals \(e_i\) are the observable counterparts to the unobservable errors \(\varepsilon_i\). We use them to check model assumptions and estimate \(\sigma^2\).

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Properties of OLS Residuals

\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n e_i = 0\) — residuals sum to zero
\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{y}_i = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i\) — sum of fitted values equals sum of observed values
\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i e_i = 0\) — residuals are uncorrelated with the predictor
\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{y}_i e_i = 0\) — residuals are uncorrelated with the fitted values
The fitted line always passes through \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\)

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text: Estimating \(\sigma^2\)

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Residual Sum of Squares
The Residual Sum of Squares (RSS) measures the total unexplained variation:
\[\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{y}_i)^2\]

A smaller RSS means the line fits the data more closely
RSS = 0 only if every point lies exactly on the fitted line

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Estimating \(\sigma^2\)
The error variance \(\sigma^2 = \text{Var}(\varepsilon_i)\) is unknown. We estimate it using the residuals.
A natural starting point is the average squared residual, but we must divide by \(n - 2\), not \(n\):
\[\widehat{\sigma}^2 = \text{MSE} = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n - 2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2}{n-2}\]
This quantity is also called the Mean Square Error (MSE).
Why \(n - 2\)? Estimating \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) uses 2 degrees of freedom since two parameters are being used.
It can be shown that \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\sigma}^2) = \sigma^2\), so \(\widehat{\sigma}^2\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\).

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Proof: Steps 1 & 2
Goal: Show \(\mathbb{E}(\text{MSE}) = \sigma^2\), i.e., \(\mathbb{E}(\text{RSS}) = (n-2)\sigma^2\).

Step 1 — rewrite RSS. Substitute \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\) to center the residuals:



Step 2 — expand the square. Use \(\sum(y_i-\bar{y})(x_i-\bar{x}) = \widehat{\beta}_1 S_{xx}\), then take expectations:

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Proof: Step 3 — Piece 1

Evaluate Piece 1: \(\mathbb{E}\!\left(\sum(y_i - \bar{y})^2\right)\)
Substitute \(y_i - \bar{y} = \beta_1(x_i - \bar{x}) + (\varepsilon_i - \bar{\varepsilon})\) and expand the square:










Recall: Model Assumptions


\(\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i) = 0\) is a model assumption (errors are mean-zero). Then by linearity of expectation: \(\mathbb{E}(\bar{\varepsilon}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i) = 0\).
Since both means are zero, \(\mathbb{E}(Z^2) = \text{Var}(Z) + [\mathbb{E}(Z)]^2\) simplifies to \(\mathbb{E}(Z^2) = \text{Var}(Z)\):
\[\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i^2) = \text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathbb{E}(\bar{\varepsilon}^2) = \text{Var}(\bar{\varepsilon}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\]

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Proof: Step 3 — Piece 2

Evaluate Piece 2: \(\mathbb{E}\!\left(\widehat{\beta}_1^2\, S_{xx}\right)\)
Since \(S_{xx}\) is non-random, this reduces to finding \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1^2)\).
Use the identity: \(\mathbb{E}(Z^2) = \text{Var}(Z) + \left[\mathbb{E}(Z)\right]^2\)

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Proof: Step 4 — Combine

We now have both pieces:
\[\text{Piece 1} = \mathbb{E}\!\left(\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2\right) = \beta_1^2 S_{xx} + (n-1)\sigma^2\]
\[\text{Piece 2} = \mathbb{E}\!\left(\widehat{\beta}_1^2 S_{xx}\right) = \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}\]
Plug them into \(\mathbb{E}(\text{RSS}) = \text{Piece 1} - \text{Piece 2}\):






\(\mathbb{E}(\text{MSE}) = \mathbb{E}\!\left(\dfrac{\text{RSS}}{n-2}\right) =\)

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Proof: Steps 1 & 2 (Solution)

Step 1 — rewrite RSS. Substitute \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\):
\[\text{RSS} = \sum(y_i - \widehat{y}_i)^2 = \sum\!\left[(y_i - \bar{y}) - \widehat{\beta}_1(x_i - \bar{x})\right]^2\]
Step 2 — expand the square. Since \(\sum(y_i-\bar{y})(x_i-\bar{x}) = \widehat{\beta}_1 S_{xx}\):
\[= \sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2 - 2\widehat{\beta}_1^2 S_{xx} + \widehat{\beta}_1^2 S_{xx} = \sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2 - \widehat{\beta}_1^2 S_{xx}\]

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Proof: Step 3 — Piece 1 (Solution)

Evaluate Piece 1: \(\mathbb{E}\!\left(\sum(y_i - \bar{y})^2\right)\)
Substitute \(y_i - \bar{y} = \beta_1(x_i-\bar{x}) + (\varepsilon_i - \bar{\varepsilon})\) and expand:
\[\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2 = \beta_1^2 S_{xx} + 2\beta_1\!\sum(x_i-\bar{x})(\varepsilon_i-\bar{\varepsilon}) + \sum(\varepsilon_i-\bar{\varepsilon})^2\]
Taking expectations — the cross term vanishes since \(\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i - \bar\varepsilon) = 0\):
\[\mathbb{E}\!\left(\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2\right) = \beta_1^2 S_{xx} + (n-1)\sigma^2\]

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Proof: Step 3 — Piece 2 (Solution)

Evaluate Piece 2: \(\mathbb{E}\!\left(\widehat{\beta}_1^2\, S_{xx}\right)\)
Since \(S_{xx}\) is non-random: \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1^2 S_{xx}) = S_{xx} \cdot \mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1^2)\).
Apply \(\mathbb{E}(Z^2) = \text{Var}(Z) + [\mathbb{E}(Z)]^2\) with \(Z = \widehat{\beta}_1\):
\[\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1^2) = \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) + \left[\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1)\right]^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} + \beta_1^2\]
Therefore: \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1^2 S_{xx}) = \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}\)

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Proof: Step 4 — Combine (Solution)

Now plug both pieces in:
\[\mathbb{E}(\text{RSS}) = \Big[\beta_1^2 S_{xx} + (n-1)\sigma^2\Big] - \Big[\sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}\Big]\]
The \(\beta_1^2 S_{xx}\) terms cancel, leaving:
\[= (n-1)\sigma^2 - \sigma^2 = (n-2)\sigma^2\]
\[\mathbb{E}(\text{MSE}) = \mathbb{E}\!\left(\frac{\text{RSS}}{n-2}\right) = \frac{(n-2)\sigma^2}{n-2} = \sigma^2 \qquad \]

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
The Residual Standard Deviation
Taking the square root gives the residual standard deviation:
\[\widehat{\sigma} = \sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}^2} = \sqrt{\frac{\text{RSS}}{n-2}}\]
Interpretation: \(\widehat{\sigma}\) is the typical size of a prediction error, on the scale of \(y\).






Tip


Compare \(\widehat{\sigma}\) to the spread of \(y\) to gauge model usefulness. A small \(\widehat{\sigma}\) relative to the range of \(y\) indicates a good fit.

title: Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Standard Errors of the Estimators
Since \(\sigma^2\) is unknown, we replace it with \(\widehat{\sigma}^2\) in the variance formulas:
\[\widehat{\text{Var}}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\widehat{\sigma}^2}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \widehat{\text{Var}}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \widehat{\sigma}^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\]
The standard errors are the square roots:
\[\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\widehat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}, \qquad \text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \widehat{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}}\]
Standard errors quantify the uncertainty in each estimate — they are the basis for confidence intervals and hypothesis tests (coming soon).

Lecture 4: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Summary

Residuals \(e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\) are observed proxies for the unobservable errors \(\varepsilon_i\)
Five properties of OLS residuals follow from the normal equations: \(\sum e_i = 0\), \(\sum \widehat{y}_i = \sum y_i\), \(\sum x_i e_i = 0\), \(\sum \widehat{y}_i e_i = 0\), and the line passes through \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\)
RSS \(= \sum e_i^2\) measures total unexplained variation — OLS minimizes it by construction
\(\widehat{\sigma}^2 = \text{RSS}/(n-2)\) is an unbiased estimate of \(\sigma^2\); dividing by \(n-2\) corrects for two constraints placed on the residuals
\(\widehat{\sigma}\) is the residual standard deviation — the typical prediction error on the scale of \(y\)
Standard errors replace \(\sigma\) with \(\widehat{\sigma}\) in the variance formulas
Use lm() in R to fit the model and summary(), residuals(), sigma() to extract results

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Review: The Simple Linear Model
From Monday, the simple linear regression model is:
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \quad \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}\sim N(0, \sigma^2)\]

\(\beta_1\) is expected change in \(y\) per one-unit increase in \(x\)
\(\beta_0\) is expected value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\)
The fitted line \(\widehat{y} = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x\) summarizes the relationship

Today: How do we estimate \(\widehat{\beta}_0\), \(\widehat{\beta}_1\), and \(\sigma\) from data?

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Learning Objectives

By the end of today you will be able to:

Explain the least squares criterion and define the residual sum of squares
Derive the OLS estimators \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) by solving the normal equations
Compute fitted values and residuals from the estimated line
Connect \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) to the sample correlation between \(x\) and \(y\)
Show that the OLS estimators are linear combinations of \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\)
Show that the OLS estimators are unbiased: \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \beta_0\) and \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\)

Mini Refresher: Derivatives
Power rule: \(\frac{d}{dx} x^n = nx^{n-1}\)
Chain rule: \(\frac{d}{dx} f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)\)
Partial derivatives: treat all other variables as constants and differentiate with respect to one variable at a time.
Example: \(\dfrac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0}(y - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x)^2 = 2(y - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x) \cdot (-1)\)

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Mini Refresher: Summation Rules
Derivatives through sums: \[\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(\beta_0) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0} f_i(\beta_0)\]
Constants in sums:

\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n c = nc\) — a constant summed \(n\) times is just \(n \times c\)
\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n c \cdot x_i = c\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\) — a constant factor pulls out of the sum







Note


These are all we need to minimize RSS — apply the chain rule, pass the derivative through the sum, set to zero, and simplify.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
How do we pick \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)?
We need a rule to pick the “best” \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\). To do so, we want to make prediction errors small across all observations simultaneously.
The residual for observation \(i\) is: \[e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\]
where \(\widehat{y}_i\) is the predicted value \(\widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i\)
To find the best line, we minimize the Residual Sum of Squares: \[\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{y}_i)^2\]
We square the residuals so positive and negative errors don’t cancel, and so large errors are penalized more heavily.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
The Least Squares Criterion
From the previous slide, \(e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\). Since the candidate line predicts \(\widehat{y}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\), substituting gives:
\[e_i = y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\]
So the Residual Sum of Squares is:
\[\text{RSS}(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\]
Goal: choose \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) to minimize RSS.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
The Normal Equations
We have 2 unknowns (\(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)) and need 2 equations to pin them down.
Setting \(\dfrac{\partial \text{RSS}}{\partial \beta_0} = 0\) and \(\dfrac{\partial \text{RSS}}{\partial \beta_1} = 0\) each gives one equation — together they form a system of two linear equations called the normal equations.
Recall: \(\text{RSS}(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\)
Strategy: differentiate RSS with respect to each parameter, set each derivative to zero, then use the chain rule and summation rule to simplify.

Set \(\partial\text{RSS}/\partial\beta_0 = 0\): \[\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = 0\]
Pass derivative through sum (summation rule): \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = 0\]
Chain rule: \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} 2(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) \cdot (-1) = 0\]
Factor out \(-2\), then divide both sides by \(-2\): \[\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0\]

Set \(\partial\text{RSS}/\partial\beta_1 = 0\): \[\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = 0\]
Pass derivative through sum (summation rule): \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_1}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = 0\]
Chain rule: \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} 2(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) \cdot (-x_i) = 0\]
Factor out \(-2\), then divide both sides by \(-2\): \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0\]

Solving the Normal Equations: Step 2 (cont.) (Solution)

Collect \(\beta_1\) terms on the right: \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y} = \beta_1\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2\right)\]
Divide both sides by \(\left(\sum x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2\right)\): \[\boxed{\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y}}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}}\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Equivalent Form of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\)
The numerator and denominator have a cleaner equivalent form. Expanding \(\sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})\):
\[\sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}) = \sum x_iy_i - \bar{y}\sum x_i - \bar{x}\sum y_i + n\bar{x}\bar{y}\]
Since \(\sum x_i = n\bar{x}\) and \(\sum y_i = n\bar{y}\):
\[= \sum x_iy_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y} - n\bar{x}\bar{y} + n\bar{x}\bar{y} = \sum x_iy_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y}\]
The same identity holds for the denominator: \(\displaystyle\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2 = \sum x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2\)
So the two forms are equivalent. We will use the simpler form on the next slide.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
The OLS Estimators

Solving the normal equations yields:
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\]
\[\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\]
where:
\[S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}) \quad \text{(co-variation of } x \text{ and } y \text{ around their means)}\]
\[S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \quad \text{(total spread of } x \text{ around its mean)}\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Connection to Correlation
The OLS slope has a useful rewrite in terms of correlation:
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = r \cdot \frac{s_y}{s_x}\]
where \(r\) is the sample correlation between \(x\) and \(y\), and \(s_x\), \(s_y\) are sample standard deviations.

The sign of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) always equals the sign of \(r\)
When \(r = 0\) \(\rightarrow\) slope is 0 \(\rightarrow\) no linear relationship
When \(|r| = 1\) \(\rightarrow\) all points lie exactly on a line \(\rightarrow\) perfect fit

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Properties of the OLS Estimators

Notation: \(S_{xx} = \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i - \bar{x})^2\) — total spread of the predictor; \(\sigma^2\) — true (unknown) error variance; \(\mathbb{E}(\cdot)\) — expected value; \(\text{Var}(\cdot)\) — variance.


Linear: \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) are linear functions of \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\)
Unbiased: \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \beta_0\) and \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\) — on average, the estimates recover the true parameters
Known variances: \[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\]
Gauss-Markov (BLUE): OLS has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators — no other such estimator can do better.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Summary

Least squares: OLS picks \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) to minimize \(\text{RSS} = \sum(y_i - \widehat{y}_i)^2\)
Normal equations give closed-form solutions: \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}\), \(\;\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\)
Residuals \(e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\) measure how far each observation falls from the fitted line

A few points of style can dramatically improve readability:

Text: the ‘Markdown’ in R Markdown
Now we’ll look over the text aspects of .Rmd documents.

Narrative text
You’ve probably noticed by now that headers are set off by #, ##, ### in the .Rmd document, and these are rendered in nice format in the knitted document. These are examples of text markdown elements, which are used to control the display of text in the knitted document. Some common ones are:

# header, number of hashes specifies header level
*italic text* renders in italic
**bold text** renders in bold
*, -, + set off itemize list elements

sub-item

1., 2., .. set off numbered lists
[link text](url) creates hyperlinks

These and other options are summarized in the R Markdown cheatsheet.


Mathematical notation
R Markdown documents also integrate math display using math expressions. For inline math environments, enclose expressions in $, such as $\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$, which appears as \(\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\).
Equation blocks can be created by enclosing math expressions in $$. For example, $$Y = \mathbf{X}\beta + \epsilon$$ displays as: \[Y = \mathbf{X}\beta + \epsilon\]
For a list of LaTeX math syntax, see wikibooks.

title: PSTAT 126: Regression Analysis
text:
This course covers the theory and application of linear and multiple regression, with an emphasis on using statistical computing to solve real-world problems. Topics include simple and multiple linear regression, analysis of residuals, transformations, variable and model selection (including stepwise regression), and analysis of covariance. All computing is done in R.
By the end of the quarter, you will be able to formulate, fit, and interpret regression models, diagnose violations of model assumptions, handle outliers, leverage points and multicollinearity, apply appropriate transformations, implement variable selection methods, and perform statistical inference and prediction.

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Francis Galton and Heredity

In the 1880s, Francis Galton studied the relationship between parents’ heights and their children’s heights.
His findings:

Tall parents tend to have taller children. Short parents tend to have shorter children.
Very tall parents tend to have tall children who are shorter than the parents. Very short parents tend to have shorter children who are taller than the parents.


Children’s heights “regressed” back toward the population mean.


This is the origin of the word “regression.”

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text: What is a Statistical Model?

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
What is a Statistical Model?

A statistical model is a way of describing real-world phenomena using mathematical relationships. It takes data as input and creates a structured way of understanding how variables relate to one another, and how those relationships can be used to predict an outcome.
\[y = f(x) + \varepsilon\]

\(y\): outcome of interest (response variable)
\(x\): predictor (explanatory variable)
\(f(x)\): systematic component
\(\varepsilon\): random error

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Why Regression?
Regression lets us answer questions like:

How does income relate to years of education?
Does economic growth predict election outcomes?
What is the average difference in test scores between two groups, holding other factors constant?
Given a new observation, what do we predict for \(y\)?

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
When do we use Regression?
Regression analysis is used for explaining or modelings the relationship between a response variable (\(Y\)) and one or more predictors (\(X_1,...X_p\)).
The response variable must be continuous, but the predictors can be continuous, discrete, or categorical.

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Inference vs. Prediction
Two distinct goals for regression:
Inference: understand how and why variables are related

Focus: the coefficients \(\beta_0, \beta_1\)
Questions: Is there a relationship? How strong? In what direction?
Example: Does studying more hours lead to higher exam scores, and by how much?

Prediction: produce accurate forecasts for new observations

Focus: the fitted value \(\widehat{y}\)
Questions: Given \(\widehat{x}\), what is our best guess for \(\widehat{y}\)?
Example: What exam score do we expect for a student who studies 8 hours?

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Simple Linear Regression
The simple linear regression model relates one predictor to a continuous outcome:
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i\]


\(y_i\): observed outcome for unit \(i\)
\(x_i\): predictor for unit \(i\)
\(\beta_0\) (intercept): expected value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\)
\(\beta_1\) (slope): expected change in \(y\) per one-unit increase in \(x\)
\(\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\): random error, independently and identically distributed

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Interpreting Slope and Intercept
For the Ames housing model, fitting gives: \[\widehat{\text{price}} = 13.3 + 0.111 \times \text{sqft}\]

Intercept (\(\widehat{\beta}_0 = 13.3\)): a house with 0 sq ft is predicted to sell for $13,300 — not meaningful on its own, but a necessary mathematical anchor
Slope (\(\widehat{\beta}_1 = 0.111\)): each additional square foot of living area is associated with $111 more in sale price, on average

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Summary

A statistical model decomposes an outcome into a systematic part \(f(x)\) and random error \(\varepsilon\)
Regression can be used for prediction or inference
Inference focuses on the coefficients: is there a relationship, how strong, in what direction?
Prediction focuses on \(\widehat{y}\): given new inputs, what is the best forecast?
The simple linear regression model is \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i\)
The slope \(\beta_1\) is the expected change in \(y\) per one-unit increase in \(x\)
The intercept \(\beta_0\) is the expected value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\)

title: Lecture 3: OLS Properties
text:
Properties of the OLS Estimators

Notation: \(S_{xx} = \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i - \bar{x})^2\) — total spread of the predictor; \(\sigma^2\) — true (unknown) error variance; \(\mathbb{E}(\cdot)\) — expected value; \(\text{Var}(\cdot)\) — variance.


Linear: \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) are linear functions of \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\)
Unbiased: \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \beta_0\) and \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\) — on average, the estimates recover the true parameters
Known variances: \[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\]
Gauss-Markov (BLUE): OLS has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators — no other such estimator can do better.

title: Lecture 3: OLS Properties
text:
Implications of the SLR Model
Under the SLR model \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i\):

\(\mathbb{E}(Y_i) = \mathbb{E}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i\) — the regression function (line)

\(\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i) = 0\) (errors are mean-zero by assumption)
\(\beta_0\) is the intercept: the value of \(\mathbb{E}(Y)\) when \(X = 0\)
\(\beta_1\) is the slope: the change in \(\mathbb{E}(Y)\) for a one-unit increase in \(X\)

\(\text{Var}(Y_i) = \text{Var}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i) = \text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2\) — the responses \(Y_i\) all have the same variance \(\sigma^2\)
\(\text{Cov}(Y_i, Y_j) = \text{Cov}(\varepsilon_i, \varepsilon_j) = 0\) — different responses are uncorrelated

text:
Property 4: Gauss-Markov (BLUE) (Solution)

Goal: OLS has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators.
Let \(b_1^* = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i y_i\) be any competing linear unbiased estimator of \(\beta_1\).
Step 1 — unbiasedness constraints. We need \(\mathbb{E}(b_1^*) = \beta_1\) for all \(\beta_0, \beta_1\). Substitute \(\mathbb{E}(y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\): \[\mathbb{E}(b_1^*) = \mathbb{E}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n c_i y_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i\,\mathbb{E}(y_i) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i) = \beta_0\sum_{i=1}^n c_i + \beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i\]
For this to equal \(\beta_1\) for every possible \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), we match coefficients: \[\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i}_{\text{coeff. of }\beta_0} = 0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i}_{\text{coeff. of }\beta_1} = 1\]

text:
Property 4: Gauss-Markov (BLUE) (cont.) (Solution)

Step 2 (cont.) — show \(\sum a_i d_i = 0\). We need this so the cross term vanishes when we expand \(\sum(a_i + d_i)^2\) in Step 3 — without it we can’t isolate \(\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1)\). Using \(\sum d_i = 0\) and \(\sum d_i x_i = 0\): \[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i d_i = \frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})d_i}{S_{xx}} = \frac{\sum d_i x_i - \bar{x}\sum d_i}{S_{xx}} = \frac{0 - 0}{S_{xx}} = 0\]

text:
Property 4: Gauss-Markov (BLUE) (cont.) (Solution)

Step 3 — compare variances. Two key rules:

\(\text{Var}(cY) = c^2\text{Var}(Y)\) — a constant scales variance by its square
\(\text{Var}(Y_1 + Y_2) = \text{Var}(Y_1) + \text{Var}(Y_2)\) when \(Y_1, Y_2\) are independent (cross terms \(2c_ic_j\text{Cov}(y_i,y_j) = 0\))

Applying both to \(b_1^* = \sum c_i y_i\) with independent \(y_i\)’s and \(\text{Var}(y_i) = \sigma^2\): \[\text{Var}(b_1^*) = \text{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n c_i y_i\right) \overset{\text{indep.}}{=} \sum_{i=1}^n \text{Var}(c_i y_i) \overset{\text{Var}(cY)=c^2\text{Var}(Y)}{=} \sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2\,\text{Var}(y_i) = \sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2\]

title: Lecture 3: OLS Properties
text:
Property 4: Gauss-Markov (BLUE) (cont.) (Solution)

Substitute \(c_i = a_i + d_i\) and expand: \[\sigma^2\sum(a_i + d_i)^2 = \sigma^2\!\left(\sum a_i^2 + 2\underbrace{\sum a_i d_i}_{=\;0} + \sum d_i^2\right) = \sigma^2\sum a_i^2 + \sigma^2\sum d_i^2\]
Recognizing \(\sigma^2 \sum a_i^2 = \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1)\): \[\text{Var}(b_1^*) = \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) + \underbrace{\sigma^2 \sum d_i^2}_{\geq\;0} \;\geq\; \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) \qquad \]
The extra term \(\sigma^2\sum d_i^2 \geq 0\) always — with equality only when \(d_i = 0\) for all \(i\), i.e. when \(b_1^* = \widehat{\beta}_1\).

title: Lecture 3: OLS Properties
text:
Summary

Property 1 (Linearity): \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) are linear combinations of \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\) with weights depending only on \(x\)
Property 2 (Unbiasedness): \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \beta_0\) and \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\) — the estimators are correct on average
Property 3 (Known variances): \(\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sigma^2/S_{xx}\), \(\;\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \sigma^2(1/n + \bar{x}^2/S_{xx})\)
Property 4 (Gauss-Markov): OLS is BLUE — smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
OLS to MLE
Where we’ve been: OLS gives us estimates \(\widehat{\beta}_0\), \(\widehat{\beta}_1\), and \(\widehat{\sigma}^2\) by minimizing the sum of squared residuals. Under the Gauss-Markov assumptions, these are the best linear unbiased estimators, but that’s all we know about them.
The gap: OLS tells us where our estimates land, but not how uncertain they are. To answer questions like “is \(\beta_1\) significantly different from zero?” or “what’s a plausible range for the true slope?”, we need to know the full distribution of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\), not just its mean and variance.
The pivot: To get those distributions, we need to make a stronger assumption. We need to assume that the errors are normally distributed. Once we do, we can use maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), a general-purpose estimation framework that requires specifying the full distribution of the data.
The payoff: It turns out MLE gives us the same estimates for \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) as OLS. But by going through MLE, we learn exactly what distribution \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) follows, allowing us to build confidence intervals and run hypothesis tests.

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text: Distribution Refresher

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
What Is a Distribution?
A probability distribution describes how the values of a random variable are spread out. It tells you which outcomes are possible and how likely each one is.
For a continuous random variable \(X\), the distribution is described by a probability density function (PDF) \(f(x)\), where:

\(f(x) \geq 0\) for all \(x\)
\(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, dx = 1\) (total probability = 1)
\(P(a \leq X \leq b) = \displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\, dx\)

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
The Normal Distribution
A random variable \(Z\) follows a normal distribution \(Z \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) if its density is
\[f(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\!\left\{-\frac{(z-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right\}\]
Key facts:

\(E(Z) = \mu\), \(\quad \text{Var}(Z) = \sigma^2\)
Symmetric and bell-shaped around \(\mu\)
The standard normal \(Z \sim N(0,1)\) has mean 0 and variance 1
Linear combinations of independent normals are normal: if \(Z_1 \sim N(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2)\) and \(Z_2 \sim N(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2)\) independently, then \[aZ_1 + bZ_2 \sim N(a\mu_1 + b\mu_2,\; a^2\sigma_1^2 + b^2\sigma_2^2)\]

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
The Chi-Squared Distribution

Where it comes from: Start with standard normals and square them.
If \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_k \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0,1)\), then squaring and summing gives:
\[V = Z_1^2 + Z_2^2 + \cdots + Z_k^2 \sim \chi^2_k\]
Why does squaring matter?

\(Z\) can be negative; \(Z^2\) is always \(\geq 0\) — so \(\chi^2\) lives on \([0, \infty)\)
Squaring also kills the symmetry: small values pile up near 0 and the distribution is right-skewed
\(k\) is the degrees of freedom: the number of squared normals you added

Key facts:

\(E(V) = k\) (average value grows with the number of terms)
Right-skewed; values are always \(\geq 0\)
Additive: if \(V_1 \sim \chi^2_{k_1}\) and \(V_2 \sim \chi^2_{k_2}\) independently, then \(V_1 + V_2 \sim \chi^2_{k_1 + k_2}\)

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
The \(t\) Distribution

Where it comes from: Combine the two previous distributions — a standard normal on top, the square root of a scaled \(\chi^2\) on the bottom:
\[T = \frac{Z}{\left(V/k\right)^{1/2}} \sim t_k \qquad Z \sim N(0,1),\quad V \sim \chi^2_k\]
How the pieces fit together:

The numerator \(Z \sim N(0,1)\) measures how far an estimate is from its true value, in standard units
The denominator \((V/k)^{1/2}\) with \(V \sim \chi^2_k\) estimates the spread

Since \(\chi^2\) is built from squared normals, it is measuring variability in the same underlying normal errors

Dividing by something random (rather than a fixed constant) inflates the tails beyond the normal

Key facts:

\(E(T) = 0\) for \(k > 1\)
\(\text{Var}(T) = \dfrac{k}{k-2}\) for \(k > 2\)
Symmetric and bell-shaped, but with heavier tails than \(N(0,1)\)

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
Why These Distributions?
So far we have been doing point estimation — finding \(\widehat{\beta}_0\), \(\widehat{\beta}_1\), and \(\widehat{\sigma}^2\) without any distributional assumption.
For inference (hypothesis tests and confidence intervals) we need to know the distribution of our estimators.

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
The Normality Assumption

The simple linear regression model is
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n\]
New assumption: the errors \(\varepsilon_i\) are iid \(N(0, \sigma^2)\).
This is stronger than the Gauss-Markov assumptions:







Gauss-Markov (OLS is BLUE)
+ Normality (enables inference)




\(E(\varepsilon_i) = 0\)
\(\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\)


\(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2\)
(implies mean 0 and constant variance)


Errors uncorrelated (no linear relationship)
Errors independent ( no relationship of any kind)



Under the normality assumption,
\[Y_i \sim N(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i,\; \sigma^2)\]

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
Maximum Likelihood Estimation (Solution)

The general PDF for \(Y \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\): \(\quad f(Y) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\!\left\{-\dfrac{(Y - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right\}\)
Step 1: Substitute \(\mu = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i\):
\[f_i(Y_i) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\!\left\{-\frac{(Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right\}\]
Step 2: Multiply the individual densities — the likelihood function:
\[L(\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma^2) = \prod_{i=1}^n f_i(Y_i) = \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{n/2}} \exp\!\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2\right\}\]
Step 3: Choose \((\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma^2)\) to maximize \(L\) — find the parameter values that make the observed data as probable as possible.

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
PDF vs. Likelihood

The PDF and the likelihood function use the same equation but differ in what you treat as known.
PDF: parameters are known, data is unknown

You know the class average is 75 and the SD is 10. How probable is a score of 80?

Likelihood: data is known, parameters are unknown

You observed scores of 72, 68, 80, 75. Which mean and SD make these four scores most probable?

In regression, we have already collected the data. So we use the likelihood. We fix the \(Y_i\)’s and search over \((\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma^2)\) to find the values that best explain what we observed.

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
The Log-Likelihood (Steps 1–2, Solution)

Maximizing \(L\) directly means differentiating a product of \(n\) exponentials, which can be messy! Taking the log turns that product into a sum, which is much easier to differentiate.
Step 1: Write \(\ell = \log L\):
\[\ell = \log L = \log \left[ \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{n/2}} \exp\!\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2\right\} \right]\]
Step 2: Split using \(\log(AB) = \log A + \log B\):
\[= \log\!\left(\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{n/2}}\right) + \log\!\left(\exp\!\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2\right\}\right)\]

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
The Log-Likelihood (Steps 3–4, Solution)

Step 3: Apply \(\log(x^a) = a\log x\) and \(\log(e^a) = a\):
\[= -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2\]
Step 4: Expand \(\log(2\pi\sigma^2) = \log(2\pi) + \log(\sigma^2)\):
\[\ell(\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma^2) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\log\sigma^2 - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2\]
To find the MLE, take partial derivatives of \(\ell\) with respect to each parameter and set them to zero.

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
Derivatives of the Log-Likelihood: \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) (Solution)

Take partial derivatives of \(\ell = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\log\sigma^2 - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2\) and set each to zero.
Step 1: \(\partial \ell / \partial \beta_0 = 0\), chain rule gives:
\[\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i) = 0\]
Step 2: \(\partial \ell / \partial \beta_1 = 0\) chain rule brings down \(X_i\):
\[\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i(Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i) = 0\]
Step 3: Since \(\sigma^2 > 0\), multiply both sides by \(\sigma^2\) (valid — cancels it):
\[\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i) = 0 \qquad \sum_{i=1}^n X_i(Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i) = 0\]
These are exactly the OLS normal equations — so MLE and OLS give the same \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)!

Take the partial derivative of \(\ell = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\log\sigma^2 - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2\) with respect to \(\sigma^2\).

Step 1: Apply the rules to each term and set to zero:

Starting from: \(\quad -n\sigma^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2 = 0\)
Step 3: Move \(n\sigma^2\) to the other side and recognize the left-hand summation:



Step 4: Divide both sides by \(n\) to solve for \(\sigma^2\), then substitute in \(\widehat{\beta}_0\), \(\widehat{\beta}_1\):

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
Derivatives of the Log-Likelihood: \(\sigma^2\) (Steps 1–2, Solution)

Take the partial derivative of \(\ell = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\log\sigma^2 - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2\) with respect to \(\sigma^2\).
Two derivative rules needed: \(\quad\dfrac{d}{dx}\log x = \dfrac{1}{x} \qquad \dfrac{d}{dx}\dfrac{1}{x} = -\dfrac{1}{x^2}\)
Step 1: Apply the rules to each term and set to zero:
\[\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \sigma^2} = -\frac{n}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{2\sigma^4}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2 = 0\]
Step 2: Multiply both sides by \(2\sigma^4\) (valid since \(\sigma^4 > 0\)):
\[-n\sigma^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2 = 0\]

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
Derivatives of the Log-Likelihood: \(\sigma^2\) (Steps 3–4, Solution)

Starting from: \(\quad -n\sigma^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2 = 0\)
Step 3: Move \(n\sigma^2\) to the other side — the left-hand summation is RSS by definition:
\[\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2}_{\text{RSS}} = n\sigma^2\]
Step 4: Divide both sides by \(n\) to solve for \(\sigma^2\):
\[\sigma^2 = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n}\]
Substitute in \(\widehat{\beta}_0\), \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) to get the MLE estimate:
\[\widehat{\sigma}^2_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n}\]

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
section: MLE vs. OLS: What’s the Same, What’s Different
text:
MLE vs. OLS: What’s the Same, What’s Different










OLS
MLE (under normality)




Goal
Minimize \(\sum(Y_i - \widehat{Y}_i)^2\)
Maximize \(L(\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma^2)\)


\(\widehat{\beta}_0\)
\(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{X}\)
\(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{X}\)


\(\widehat{\beta}_1\)
\(\widehat{\beta}_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}\)
\(\widehat{\beta}_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}\)


\(\widehat{\sigma}^2\)
\(\text{MSE} = \text{RSS}/(n-2)\) — unbiased
\(\text{RSS}/n\) — biased



Why \(n-2\) for OLS? To compute the residuals \(e_i = Y_i - \widehat{Y}_i\), we first had to estimate \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) from the same data. Each estimated parameter imposes one constraint on the residuals, leaving only \(n - 2\) that carry independent information about \(\sigma^2\). Dividing by \(n-2\) instead of \(n\) corrects for this and makes \(\widehat{\sigma}^2\) unbiased.
Why \(n\) for MLE? MLE maximizes the likelihood with no bias correction. It simply divides by \(n\). Because it ignores the two constraints imposed by estimating \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\), it systematically underestimates \(\sigma^2\).

title: Lecture 5: Inference in Regression
text:
Summary

Three key distributions: Normal (sums of normals), \(\chi^2\) (sums of squared standard normals), \(t\) (normal over \((\chi^2/k)^{1/2}\)) — these underpin all regression inference
Normality assumption \(\varepsilon_i \sim N(0,\sigma^2)\) is needed for inference; it strengthens the Gauss-Markov setup
MLE agrees with OLS for \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) under normality
MLE of \(\sigma^2\) is biased (divides by \(n\))

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Where We Left Off
Last lecture, we added the normality assumption \(\varepsilon_i \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)\), which implies:
\[Y_i \sim N(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i,\ \sigma^2)\]
We used MLE to show:

\(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) from MLE equal the OLS estimates
The MLE of \(\sigma^2\) is biased — it divides by \(n\), not \(n-2\)

Today: We use the full distributional setup to derive exact distributions for \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) and build confidence intervals and hypothesis tests from them.

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text: Inference on \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Sampling Distribution of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\)
The OLS slope can be written as a weighted sum of the \(Y_i\)’s:
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n \underbrace{\frac{X_i - \bar{X}}{S_{xx}}}_{c_i} Y_i \qquad \text{where } S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2\]

Since each \(Y_i \sim N(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i, \sigma^2)\), and a linear combination of independent normals is normal, we need only find the mean and variance.
We showed earlier: \(E(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\) and \(\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\)
\[\boxed{\widehat{\beta}_1 \sim N\!\left(\beta_1,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}\]

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
From Normal to \(t\): The Problem
Standardizing \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) gives a standard normal:
\[\frac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{\sigma / S_{xx}^{1/2}} \sim N(0, 1)\]
The problem: \(\sigma^2\) is unknown. We replace it with \(\text{MSE} = \dfrac{\text{RSS}}{n-2}\).

Replacing a fixed constant with a random estimate inflates the tails. The result is no longer normal.
Recall from last lecture: \(T = Z / (V/k)^{1/2}\) where \(Z \sim N(0,1)\) and \(V \sim \chi^2_k\). The missing piece is showing that RSS fits the chi-squared structure in the denominator:
\[\frac{\text{RSS}}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-2} \quad \text{and is independent of } \widehat{\beta}_0 \text{ and } \widehat{\beta}_1\]

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Confidence Interval for \(\beta_1\) (Setup)
Since \(\dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{(\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2}} \sim t_{n-2}\):
Step 1: Trap the expression between \(\pm\, t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\) with probability \(1-\alpha\):



Step 2: Rearrange the inequality to isolate \(\beta_1\):



Result:

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Confidence Interval for \(\beta_1\) (Solution)

Since \(\dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{(\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2}} \sim t_{n-2}\):
Step 1: Trap the expression between \(\pm\, t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\) with probability \(1-\alpha\):
\[P\!\left(-t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2} \leq \frac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{(\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2}} \leq t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\right) = 1 - \alpha\]
Step 2: Multiply through by \((\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2}\) and flip signs to isolate \(\beta_1\):
\[P\!\left(\widehat{\beta}_1 - t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\left(\frac{\text{MSE}}{S_{xx}}\right)^{1/2} \;\leq\; \beta_1 \;\leq\; \widehat{\beta}_1 + t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\left(\frac{\text{MSE}}{S_{xx}}\right)^{1/2}\right) = 1 - \alpha\]
Result: A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\beta_1\):
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 \;\pm\; t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\left(\frac{\text{MSE}}{S_{xx}}\right)^{1/2}\]

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Interpreting and Using the CI
Correct interpretation: If we repeated the study many times, \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) of the resulting intervals would contain \(\beta_1\).

Common mistake: “There is a 95% probability that \(\beta_1\) is in this interval.” — \(\beta_1\) is a fixed (unknown) constant, not random; it either is or isn’t in any given interval.


What makes the interval wider or narrower?

Larger MSE → noisier data → wider CI
Larger \(S_{xx}\) → more spread in \(X\) → better slope estimate → narrower CI
Larger \(n\) → smaller \(t\) critical value → narrower CI



Practical use: If the CI for \(\beta_1\) does not contain 0, we have evidence that \(X\) is a useful linear predictor of \(Y\) at the chosen significance level.

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Hypothesis Test for \(\beta_1\)
To test \(H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_{10}\) (some fixed value), compute:
\[t^* = \frac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_{10}}{(\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2}}\]
Under \(H_0\), \(t^* \sim t_{n-2}\).

Decision rules at significance level \(\alpha\):







Hypotheses
Reject \(H_0\) if




\(H_1: \beta_1 \neq \beta_{10}\) (two-sided)
\(|t^*| > t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\)


\(H_1: \beta_1 > \beta_{10}\) (right-sided)
\(t^* > t_{1-\alpha,\, n-2}\)


\(H_1: \beta_1 < \beta_{10}\) (left-sided)
\(t^* < -t_{1-\alpha,\, n-2}\)

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
The Most Important Test: \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\)
\(Y\) is independent of \(X\) if and only if \(\beta_1 = 0\). Testing \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) asks: does \(X\) have any linear relationship with \(Y\) at all?
\[t^* = \frac{\widehat{\beta}_1}{(\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2}} = \frac{\widehat{\beta}_1}{\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_1)}\]

This is exactly what R reports under summary(lm(...)):

fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
summary(fit)$coefficients

             Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 37.285126   1.877627 19.857575 8.241799e-19
wt          -5.344472   0.559101 -9.559044 1.293959e-10




The t value column is \(\widehat{\beta}/\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta})\). The Pr(>|t|) column is the two-sided \(p\)-value. A small \(p\)-value is evidence against \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\).

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Inference for \(\beta_0\)

By the same argument, \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \widehat{\beta}_1 \bar{X}\) is also a linear combination of the \(Y_i\)’s:
\[\widehat{\beta}_0 \sim N\!\left(\beta_0,\ \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{X}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\right)\]

It follows that:
\[\frac{\widehat{\beta}_0 - \beta_0}{\left[\text{MSE}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\bar{X}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\right]^{1/2}} \sim t_{n-2}\]


A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\beta_0\):
\[\widehat{\beta}_0 \;\pm\; t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\left[\text{MSE}\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{X}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\right]^{1/2}\]
Hypothesis tests work exactly as they do for \(\beta_1\).

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Inference in R

fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
confint(fit, level = 0.95)

                2.5 %    97.5 %
(Intercept) 33.450500 41.119753
wt          -6.486308 -4.202635



confint() applies the CI formula to each coefficient automatically.

# manually verify the CI for the slope
b1_hat <- coef(fit)["wt"]
se_b1  <- summary(fit)$coefficients["wt", "Std. Error"]
n      <- nrow(mtcars)
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = n - 2)
b1_hat + c(-1, 1) * t_crit * se_b1

[1] -6.486308 -4.202635

After fitting \(\widehat{Y} = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 X\), we often want to say something about a new input value \(x^*\).
There are two fundamentally different questions:

Question 1 — Mean response: > “What is the average fuel efficiency for all cars weighing 3,500 lbs?”
Targets \(E(Y \mid X = x^*) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x^*\) — a fixed (unknown) parameter.
\(\longrightarrow\) Confidence interval for mean response


Question 2 — New individual observation: > “How many mpg will this specific 3,500 lb car get?”
Targets \(Y^* = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x^* + \varepsilon^*\) — a random variable with its own noise.
\(\longrightarrow\) Prediction interval


Both are centered at the same point estimate \(\widehat{Y}^* = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x^*\). They differ in what uncertainty they account for.

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Variance of the Fitted Value \(\widehat{Y}^*\)
Our point estimate at \(x^*\) is \(\widehat{Y}^* = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x^*\). It carries uncertainty from both coefficient estimates.

Since \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) share the same data, they are correlated: \(\text{Cov}(\widehat{\beta}_0, \widehat{\beta}_1) = -\bar{X}\sigma^2/S_{xx}\).
Expanding the variance of \(\widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x^*\) and substituting this covariance:
\[\text{Var}(\widehat{Y}^*) = \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x^* - \bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\]


Two things to notice:

Smallest at \(x^* = \bar{X}\) — we’re most certain about the fitted value at the center of the data
Grows as \(x^*\) moves away from \(\bar{X}\) — extrapolation compounds uncertainty

text:
Confidence Interval for Mean Response
Replacing \(\sigma^2\) with MSE gives a \(t_{n-2}\) distribution:
\[\frac{\widehat{Y}^* - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x^*)}{\left[\text{MSE}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{(x^*-\bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\right]^{1/2}} \sim t_{n-2}\]

A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(E(Y \mid X = x^*)\):
\[\boxed{\widehat{Y}^* \;\pm\; t_{1-\alpha/2,\, n-2}\left[\text{MSE}\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x^*-\bar{X})^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\right]^{1/2}}\]

section: From Normal to \(t\): Putting It Together
text:
From Normal to \(t\): Putting It Together
We have two pieces:

\(\dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{\sigma / S_{xx}^{1/2}} \sim N(0,1)\) — the standardized slope
\(\dfrac{\text{RSS}}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-2}\), independent of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) — the chi-squared denominator


Substituting \(\text{MSE} = \text{RSS}/(n-2)\) for \(\sigma^2\) and applying the \(t\)-distribution definition (\(T = Z / (V/k)^{1/2}\)):
\[\frac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1}{(\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2}} = \frac{N(0,1)}{(\chi^2_{n-2}/(n-2))^{1/2}} \sim t_{n-2}\]

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Refresher: Confidence Intervals
\(\alpha\) (significance level): the probability of making an error. Specifically, the probability that the interval fails to contain the true parameter. We choose \(\alpha\) before looking at the data. Common choices are \(0.05\) or \(0.01\).
A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI traps the true parameter between two data-driven bounds with probability \(1-\alpha\).
Key idea: choose critical values \(\pm\, t_{1-\alpha/2}\) that leave \(\alpha/2\) in each tail.

For \(\alpha = 0.05\): critical values are \(\pm\, t_{0.975,\, n-2}\), giving a 95% CI.

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
\(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\)
\(Y\) is independent of \(X\) if and only if \(\beta_1 = 0\). Testing \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) asks: does \(X\) have any linear relationship with \(Y\) at all?
\[t^* = \frac{\widehat{\beta}_1}{(\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2}} = \frac{\widehat{\beta}_1}{\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_1)}\]

This is exactly what R reports under summary(lm(...)):

fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
summary(fit)$coefficients

             Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 37.285126   1.877627 19.857575 8.241799e-19
wt          -5.344472   0.559101 -9.559044 1.293959e-10




The t value column is \(\widehat{\beta}/\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta})\). The Pr(>|t|) column is the two-sided \(p\)-value. A small \(p\)-value is evidence against \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\).

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Q1: Why Minimize Squared Residuals?
A student proposes finding the best-fitting line by minimizing \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n e_i\) instead of \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2\). Explain why this approach fails.

Minimizing \(\sum e_i\) fails because positive and negative residuals cancel out. In fact, one of the properties of OLS residuals is that \(\sum e_i = 0\) always — so this criterion places no constraint on the line at all and cannot produce a unique fit.
Squaring the residuals:

prevents cancellation
penalizes large errors more heavily
produces a unique, well-defined solution

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Q2: Inference vs. Prediction
For each scenario, state whether the primary goal is inference or prediction and justify.
(a) A researcher wants to know whether students who attend more office hours tend to earn higher exam scores, and by roughly how many points per additional visit.

→ Inference. The goal is to understand the direction and magnitude of the relationship (how many points per visit), not just produce a predicted score.


(b) An app uses a patient’s age, weight, and exercise level to estimate their resting heart rate.
→ Prediction. The goal is an accurate individual estimate — the coefficient values are not the focus.

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Q3: Errors vs. Residuals; Unbiasedness
The SLR model is \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i\).
(a) Explain the difference between the true error \(\varepsilon_i\) and the residual \(e_i\). Which one can we observe, and why?

\(\varepsilon_i\) is the true, unobservable error. It is the gap between \(y_i\) and the true line \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\).
\(e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\) is the observable residual. It is the gap between \(y_i\) and the fitted line. We can compute \(e_i\) from data; \(\varepsilon_i\) requires knowing the unknown true parameters.

Q4–5: Computing and Interpreting the Model
A sports scientist records weeks of training (\(x\)) and one-mile run time in minutes (\(y\)) for \(n = 6\) runners. Given: \(\bar{x} = 7\), \(\bar{y} = 8\), \(S_{xx} = 70\), \(S_{xy} = -70\).
Compute \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_0\). (5, 3 pts) Write the fitted equation and interpret \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) in context.
Given \(S_{xy} = -70\), \(S_{xx} = 70\), \(\bar{x} = 7\), \(\bar{y} = 8\):
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}} = \frac{-70}{70} = -1 \qquad \widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x} = 8 - (-1)(7) = 15\]

Fitted model: \(\quad\widehat{\text{time}} = 15 - 1 \cdot \text{weeks}\)
Interpretation of \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = -1\): Each additional week of training is associated with a predicted reduction of 1 minute in one-mile run time, on average.

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Q3: Errors vs. Residuals; Unbiasedness
(b) What does it mean to say the OLS estimators are unbiased? Why is unbiasedness a desirable property?

An estimator is unbiased if its expected value equals the true parameter:
\[E(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1 \qquad E(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \beta_0\]
On average across many repeated samples, the estimates are correct.

title: Lecture 7: Prediction and Intervals
text:
Summary

CI for mean response at \(x^*\): targets \(E(Y \mid X = x^*)\); uncertainty comes only from estimating \(\widehat{Y}^*\)
PI for new observation at \(x^*\): targets an individual \(Y^*\); adds \(\sigma^2\) for irreducible noise — always wider than the CI
Both intervals are centered at \(\widehat{Y}^*\) and are narrowest at \(x^* = \bar{X}\), widening with extrapolation
PI does not shrink to zero as \(n \to \infty\) — individual noise cannot be eliminated with more data
In R: predict(..., interval = "confidence") vs. predict(..., interval = "prediction")

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Practice: One-Sided Test (\(H_1: \beta_1 > \beta_{10}\))
A nutritionist believes that each additional gram of daily protein intake increases resting metabolic rate by more than 2 calories/day. She fits a regression on \(n = 20\) participants and obtains \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = 2.8\), \(S_{xx} = 500\), \(\text{MSE} = 9\).
Task: Test \(H_0: \beta_1 = 2\) vs. \(H_1: \beta_1 > 2\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).






Step 1: Compute \(\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = (\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2} = (9/500)^{1/2} \approx 0.134\)
\[t^* = \frac{\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_{10}}{(\text{MSE}/S_{xx})^{1/2}} = \frac{2.8 - 2}{0.134} \approx 5.97\]


Step 2: Right-sided test — compare to \(t_{0.95,\,18} = 1.734\):
\[t^* = 5.97 > 1.734 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{Reject } H_0\]
Conclusion: At \(\alpha = 0.05\), there is sufficient evidence that each additional gram of protein increases metabolic rate by more than 2 calories/day.

title: Lecture 6: Inference in Regression
text:
Practice: One-Sided Test (\(H_1: \beta_1 < \beta_{10}\))

An engineer claims a new insulation material reduces heat loss by fewer than 3 watts per cm of thickness. A regression on \(n = 15\) panels gives \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = -2.1\), \(S_{xx} = 200\), \(\text{MSE} = 4\).
Task: Test \(H_0: \beta_1 = -3\) vs. \(H_1: \beta_1 > -3\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).






Step 1: Compute \(\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = (4/200)^{1/2} = 0.141\)
\[t^* = \frac{-2.1 - (-3)}{0.141} = \frac{0.9}{0.141} \approx 6.38\]


Step 2: Right-sided test — compare to \(t_{0.95,\,13} = 1.771\):
\[t^* = 6.38 > 1.771 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{Reject } H_0\]
Conclusion: At \(\alpha = 0.05\), there is sufficient evidence that heat loss reduction per cm is less than 3 watts (i.e., the slope is greater than \(-3\)).
